_about: Seed concepts for the aliveness ontology (#6720). Hand-authored; `gloss`, `tradition` and `era` are scholarly background (claude-opus-5-5), not corpus findings. `forms` are spellings in the original scripts and their usual renderings, checked against the page-terms harvest by terms.mjs. `search` are the exact phrases counted in the corpus (Atlas Search phrase match over translation + OCR); a node is only as precise as these phrases, and broad ones are flagged `broad`.

kinds.principle: Principle: what is said to make a thing alive

nodes.label: pneuma
nodes.gloss: Breath or warm air, which Greek physicians made the carrier of life in the body and the Stoics made the active, intelligent principle running through the whole cosmos.

nodes.label: psychē
nodes.gloss: The soul as the principle of life. In Aristotle's De anima it is what distinguishes a living body from a dead one, with nutritive, sensitive and rational powers.

nodes.label: vegetative soul
nodes.gloss: Aristotle's lowest power of soul, shared by plants, animals and people: nutrition, growth and reproduction. Scholastic medicine kept it as the anima vegetativa.

nodes.label: entelechy
nodes.gloss: Aristotle's word for a thing's being at work in its completed form; the soul is the first entelechy of a natural body. Hans Driesch borrowed it around 1905 for the non-mechanical factor he believed directs embryonic development.

nodes.label: spiritus
nodes.gloss: The Latin rendering of pneuma: breath, the subtle vapour that carries life and sensation through the body, and in theology the Holy Spirit. Alchemists also used it for volatile distillates.

nodes.label: vital spirits
nodes.gloss: In the Galenic scheme, the spirit made in the left ventricle of the heart from air and blood, which carries innate heat and life to the body through the arteries.

nodes.label: animal spirits
nodes.gloss: The finest spirit, refined in the brain and carried through the nerves to give sensation and motion. Descartes kept the animal spirits as a purely mechanical fluid.

nodes.label: innate heat
nodes.gloss: The heat born with a living body, centred in the heart, which drives digestion and life. Aristotle and Galen held that life lasts as long as this heat is fed; old age is its waning.

nodes.label: radical moisture
nodes.gloss: The fatty, oily moisture laid down at conception which the innate heat slowly consumes, like oil in a lamp. Avicenna's teaching made it the measure of a lifespan; prolonging life meant sparing it.

nodes.label: archeus
nodes.gloss: Paracelsus's inner craftsman: an agent in each body (and in the earth) that separates the useful from the poisonous in food and shapes things into their kind. Van Helmont made it the governing spirit of every organ.

nodes.label: mumia
nodes.gloss: In Paracelsian medicine, the vital balsam that keeps flesh from decay, and the life that stays in blood, hair or a fresh corpse after it leaves the body; the basis of sympathetic cures.

nodes.label: natural balsam
nodes.gloss: Paracelsus's inner preservative of the body, which heals wounds from within and keeps flesh from corruption; physicians tried to strengthen it with balsams of their own making.

nodes.label: world soul
nodes.gloss: The soul Plato's Timaeus gives to the cosmos, which makes the universe one living animal. Plotinus, Ficino, Bruno and Schelling each restated it.

nodes.label: spirit of the world
nodes.gloss: In Ficino's De vita (1489), the subtle body linking the world soul to the world's matter. Talismans, music, scents and sunlight were thought to draw it into human spirit.

nodes.label: seminal reasons
nodes.gloss: The Stoic logoi spermatikoi: formative principles carried in the divine pneuma like seeds, from which each kind of thing grows. Augustine's rationes seminales and Paracelsian 'seeds' continue the idea.

nodes.label: quintessence
nodes.gloss: The fifth essence, incorruptible like the heavens. John of Rupescissa (c. 1350) taught that it could be drawn from wine by repeated distillation and would keep the body from decay.

nodes.label: plastic nature
nodes.gloss: Ralph Cudworth's unconscious formative power (1678) through which God orders growth and generation without direct intervention, offered against both mechanism and atheism.

nodes.label: formative drive
nodes.gloss: Johann Friedrich Blumenbach's Bildungstrieb (1781): a drive in living matter to take and keep a specific shape, to regenerate and to reproduce. Kant cited it.

nodes.label: vital principle
nodes.gloss: Paul-Joseph Barthez's principe vital (1778): the cause of the phenomena of life in the human body, distinct from both the thinking soul and the body's matter.

nodes.label: vital force
nodes.gloss: The Lebenskraft or vis vitalis of Romantic-era physiology (Reil, Hufeland): a force peculiar to organic matter that resists decay. Hufeland made its careful husbanding the basis of long life.

nodes.label: élan vital
nodes.gloss: Henri Bergson's term in L'Évolution créatrice (1907) for the impetus of life that pushes evolution into divergent, unforeseeable forms.

nodes.label: animal magnetism
nodes.gloss: Franz Anton Mesmer's universal fluid (1779), which he held fills the universe and the nerves and can be directed by a practitioner's passes to cure illness.

nodes.label: animal electricity
nodes.gloss: Luigi Galvani's electricity inherent in animal tissue (1791), shown by frog legs twitching under metal contact. Galvanic experiments on corpses followed, and the idea fed talk of reanimation.

nodes.label: odic force
nodes.gloss: Karl von Reichenbach's Od (1845), a radiance he believed sensitive people could see around magnets, crystals and bodies.

nodes.label: astral light
nodes.gloss: Éliphas Lévi's universal agent (1856), a living fluid joining all things through which imagination and will act at a distance; Theosophy took it over.

nodes.label: ruach
nodes.gloss: Wind, breath and spirit in the Hebrew Bible, the breath God gives to living things. The Septuagint renders it pneuma, so it enters Greek and Latin as spirit.

nodes.label: breath of life
nodes.gloss: The breath God blows into the nostrils of the man formed from earth, after which he becomes a living soul (nefesh chayah). It is the model scene for giving life to a made body.

nodes.label: rūḥ
nodes.gloss: Spirit in the Qur'an and in Arabic medicine. Physicians such as Avicenna used it for the vaporous spirit born in the heart; Sufis for the spirit God breathed into Adam.

nodes.label: qi
nodes.gloss: Vapour, breath and the stuff of which all things condense. In Chinese medicine it circulates in the channels; in self-cultivation it is refined and conserved to prolong life.

nodes.label: jing (essence)
nodes.gloss: Essence: the refined, generative substance stored in the kidneys and spent in sex and ageing. Daoist longevity practice aims to conserve it and refine it into qi and spirit.

nodes.label: prāṇa
nodes.gloss: Breath and the life-force. The Upaniṣads make prāṇa the support of the senses; yoga and Āyurveda divide it into five winds that move through the channels (nāḍī).

nodes.label: ojas
nodes.gloss: Vigour: in Āyurveda the finest product of digestion, which sustains immunity and life. Its loss brings decline; rasāyana therapy is meant to increase it.

nodes.label: kuṇḍalinī
nodes.gloss: The coiled power asleep at the base of the spine in tantric anatomy, which practice wakes and leads up the central channel.

nodes.label: rlung (wind)
nodes.gloss: Wind: the Tibetan rendering of Sanskrit prāṇa and vāyu. In Tibetan medicine it is one of three humours; in tantric yoga the winds carry mind through the channels.

nodes.label: mana
nodes.gloss: A power residing in persons, places and objects in Melanesian and Polynesian usage, made a general category by R. H. Codrington (1891) and later by Marett and Mauss.

nodes.label: manitou
nodes.gloss: The Algonquian word for the spirit power present in persons, animals and places, recorded by Jesuit missionaries and later anthropologists.

nodes.label: kami
nodes.gloss: The gods, spirits and awe-inspiring presences of Shintō, residing in mountains, rivers, trees, ancestors and shrines.

nodes.label: genius loci
nodes.gloss: The guardian spirit of a place in Roman religion, honoured with altars and offerings; the lares and penates of the household belong to the same family.

nodes.label: daimōn
nodes.gloss: A spirit between gods and humans: a person's guardian, a power in a place, or an intermediary carrying prayers up and gifts down, as in Plato's Symposium.

nodes.label: elemental spirits
nodes.gloss: The beings of Paracelsus's Liber de nymphis (pub. 1566): nymphs of water, sylphs of air, gnomes of earth and salamanders of fire, made of flesh but without a soul.

nodes.label: spirits of the land
nodes.gloss: The lords of the soil (sa bdag), lords of the place (gzhi bdag) and serpent spirits (klu) of Tibetan religion, who own the ground and must be placated before building or farming.

nodes.label: cosmic sympathy
nodes.gloss: The Stoic teaching that the cosmos is one body held together by pneuma, so that what happens in one part affects the others: the moon and the tides, the heavens and the body. Plotinus, Ficino and the natural magicians all built on it.

nodes.label: antipathy
nodes.gloss: The natural enmity between things (the elephant and the ram, the vine and the cabbage), the counterpart of sympathy in Pliny, Plutarch and the Renaissance books of secrets.

nodes.label: Stoic physics
nodes.gloss: Zeno, Chrysippus and their successors held that the cosmos is a living, rational animal pervaded by a fiery pneuma, the active principle that shapes passive matter.

nodes.label: Platonism and Neoplatonism
nodes.gloss: Plato's Timaeus gives the cosmos a soul. Plotinus and Proclus place soul between intellect and matter; Ficino's Florentine translations (1460s–1490s) carried this into Renaissance medicine and magic.

nodes.label: Hermetism
nodes.gloss: The teaching of the Greek and Latin texts ascribed to Hermes Trismegistus. The Asclepius describes Egyptian priests drawing spirits into statues; the Corpus Hermeticum calls the cosmos a living being.

nodes.label: Galenic medicine
nodes.gloss: Medicine built on Galen's synthesis: four humours, innate heat, three spirits (natural, vital, animal) and the regimen of the six non-naturals, transmitted through Arabic and Latin schools.

nodes.label: Paracelsian medicine
nodes.gloss: Paracelsus (1493–1541) and his followers replaced the humours with chemical principles (salt, sulphur, mercury), made the archeus the agent of life, and prepared medicines by chemical separation.

nodes.label: Helmontian medicine
nodes.gloss: Jan Baptist van Helmont's system (Ortus medicinae, 1648): water as the one material element, seeds and archei as the agents of form, ferments as the means of change.

nodes.label: Cambridge Platonism
nodes.gloss: Henry More, Ralph Cudworth and their circle, who defended an active spiritual nature in the world against Hobbes and the mechanical philosophy. More called it the spirit of nature.

nodes.label: Stahl's animism
nodes.gloss: Georg Ernst Stahl's Theoria medica vera (1708): the rational soul itself directs every vital motion and resists the body's tendency to rot. Against mechanism, which treated the body as a machine.

nodes.label: Montpellier vitalism
nodes.gloss: The medical school of Montpellier (Bordeu, Barthez, later Lordat), which explained health and illness by a vital principle and the sensibility of each organ, not by mechanics or a rational soul.

nodes.label: vitalism
nodes.gloss: The view, under many names, that living things are governed by a principle not reducible to physics and chemistry. The word itself is 19th-century and was mostly used by opponents.

nodes.label: Naturphilosophie
nodes.gloss: Schelling's philosophy of nature (Von der Weltseele, 1798) and its school, which read nature as a self-organising whole and polarity as the law of life.

nodes.label: Bergson's creative evolution
nodes.gloss: Bergson's account of life as duration and invention, driven by the élan vital, set against both mechanism and finalism.

nodes.label: hylozoism
nodes.gloss: The view that matter itself is alive. Cudworth coined the word (1678) for a position he rejected and pinned it on Strato and the early Ionians.

nodes.label: panpsychism
nodes.gloss: The view that mind or soul is present in everything. Francesco Patrizi coined panpsychia (1591); Fechner and others revived it in the 19th century.

nodes.label: animism
nodes.gloss: E. B. Tylor's term (Primitive Culture, 1871) for belief in spiritual beings, which he took to be the root of religion; the label was later applied to many traditions that did not use it.

nodes.label: microcosm and macrocosm
nodes.gloss: The human being as a small world mirroring the great one, organ for planet and humour for element. Paracelsus and Fludd built medicine on the correspondence.

nodes.label: spontaneous generation
nodes.gloss: The birth of living things (insects, frogs, eels) from mud, dew or rotting matter without parents, accepted from Aristotle to the 17th century and tested by Redi (1668) and Pasteur (1862).

nodes.label: growth of metals
nodes.gloss: The belief that metals grow and ripen in the earth like fruit, so that mines regenerate when left to rest and alchemy can speed the ripening.

nodes.label: Daoist body cultivation
nodes.gloss: The family of Daoist teachings (Zhuangzi, the Baopuzi, the Shangqing and Quanzhen schools) that treat the body as a store of essence, qi and spirit to be refined toward long life and transcendence.

nodes.label: Āyurveda
nodes.gloss: The 'knowledge of long life' of the Caraka and Suśruta compendia: three doṣas, the tissues (dhātu) and ojas, with rasāyana as the branch devoted to rejuvenation.

nodes.label: haṭha yoga
nodes.gloss: The yoga of force, codified in texts such as the Haṭhapradīpikā (15th c.): postures, breath retention, seals and locks to move prāṇa and bindu, with freedom from ageing among its promised fruits.

nodes.label: Tibetan medicine
nodes.gloss: Sowa rigpa, the 'science of healing', codified in the Four Tantras (rgyud bzhi): three humours (wind, bile, phlegm) and a branch of rejuvenation (bcud len).

nodes.label: mechanical philosophy
nodes.gloss: The 17th-century programme (Descartes, Gassendi, Boyle, Hobbes) that explained nature by matter in motion, removing souls and inner powers from bodies.

nodes.label: regimen of health
nodes.gloss: Management of the six non-naturals (air, food and drink, sleep and waking, exercise and rest, evacuation, passions of the soul) to keep innate heat and moisture in balance. The Regimen sanitatis Salernitanum is its best-known handbook.

nodes.label: the sober life
nodes.gloss: Alvise Cornaro's Discorsi della vita sobria (1558): after a dissolute youth he ate twelve ounces of food a day, lived past ninety by his own account, and wrote about it in old age.

nodes.label: prolongation of life
nodes.gloss: The project, from Roger Bacon's De retardatione accidentium senectutis to Francis Bacon's Historia vitae et mortis (1623), of slowing old age by conserving the body's spirits and moisture.

nodes.label: macrobiotics
nodes.gloss: Christoph Wilhelm Hufeland's Die Kunst, das menschliche Leben zu verlängern (1796), retitled Makrobiotik from the 1805 edition: a long life comes from husbanding the vital force through moderation, fresh air and calm.
search: Kunst das menschliche Leben zu verlängern

nodes.label: care of old age
nodes.gloss: Gerocomia, the branch of regimen for the old, from Galen's book on hygiene to Zerbi's Gerontocomia (1489): warm moist foods, wine, rest and rubbing to slow the drying of age.

nodes.label: medical gymnastics
nodes.gloss: Exercise as part of regimen, from Hippocratic and Galenic writings to Mercuriale's De arte gymnastica (1569), meant to warm the body, stir the spirits and preserve health.

nodes.label: elixir of life
nodes.gloss: From Arabic al-iksīr: the medicine that perfects metals and, taken by people, cures illness and lengthens life. The Latin West called it elixir vitae.

nodes.label: potable gold
nodes.gloss: Gold dissolved into a drinkable liquid, prescribed because gold does not decay and was thought to pass that quality to the body; Francis Anthony sold it in 1600s London.

nodes.label: universal medicine
nodes.gloss: The philosophers' stone taken as a medicine for every disease and for the restoration of youth: the panacea or medicina universalis.

nodes.label: water of life
nodes.gloss: Aqua vitae, the distilled spirit of wine, which Arnald of Villanova and Rupescissa praised as a preserver of youth; in Persian and Arabic legend, the spring of life (āb-i ḥayāt) that Khiḍr found and Alexander missed.

nodes.label: spagyric medicine
nodes.gloss: Paracelsian pharmacy that separates a plant or mineral into its principles and recombines the purified parts, to free the medicinal virtue from the dead body of the matter.

nodes.label: palingenesis of plants
nodes.gloss: The experiment, reported by Quercetanus, Kircher and Digby, of making the ghostly form of a burnt plant rise again from its salts in a sealed glass.

nodes.label: weapon salve and powder of sympathy
nodes.gloss: Healing a wound by anointing the weapon that made it, or by treating a bloodied cloth with powder of vitriol, at a distance. Its defenders (Goclenius, Fludd, Digby) explained it by sympathy carried through the blood's spirit.

nodes.label: natural magic
nodes.gloss: The use of the hidden powers of things, which act through sympathy, to produce wonders without demons. Ficino, Agrippa and Della Porta's Magia naturalis (1558) are its main books.

nodes.label: talismans
nodes.gloss: Images cut or cast at an astrologically chosen hour so that a star's power enters them. The Picatrix (Ghāyat al-ḥakīm) and Ficino's De vita coelitus comparanda describe the making.

nodes.label: ensouling statues
nodes.gloss: The Asclepius says Egyptian priests made gods by drawing spirits into statues with herbs, stones and songs. Iamblichus and Proclus called this the telestic art; Ficino quoted the passage.

nodes.label: installing life in images
nodes.gloss: Rites that make an image a living presence: Hindu prāṇapratiṣṭhā, the 'establishing of breath' in a temple image, and Tibetan rab gnas, the consecration that installs a deity in a statue or stūpa.

nodes.label: golem
nodes.gloss: A figure of clay animated by divine names, following instructions read into the Sefer Yetzirah by medieval commentators. Later legends tie it to Rabbi Loew of Prague.

nodes.label: homunculus
nodes.gloss: The little man that De natura rerum (attributed to Paracelsus, pub. 1572) says can be grown from human seed in horse dung and fed on blood.

nodes.label: offerings to place spirits
nodes.gloss: Gifts that keep the owners of a place well disposed: the Tibetan smoke offering (bsang) and serpent-spirit rites, the Roman lararium, the Chinese earth-god shrine.

nodes.label: prāṇāyāma
nodes.gloss: Control and lengthening of the breath, the fourth limb of Patañjali's yoga; in haṭha texts it holds prāṇa in the body and is said to delay death.

nodes.label: tummo (inner heat)
nodes.gloss: The first of the Six Yogas of Nāropa: kindling a fire at the navel with breath and visualisation, melting the drops in the channels and producing bliss and bodily heat.

nodes.label: rasāyana
nodes.gloss: The Āyurvedic branch of rejuvenation: herbal and later mineral and mercurial preparations to restore youth, strengthen ojas and lengthen life. In tantric alchemy (rasaśāstra) it extends to bodily immortality.

nodes.label: kāyakalpa
nodes.gloss: Rejuvenation of the body by a long secluded course of fasting, herbal and mineral medicines, after which the patient is said to grow new teeth, hair and skin.

nodes.label: chülen (essence extraction)
nodes.gloss: Tibetan bcud len, 'taking the essence', the translation of rasāyana: pills of flowers, stones or minerals taken in retreat to live without ordinary food and restore the body.

nodes.label: yangsheng (nourishing life)
nodes.gloss: Nourishing life: diet, breathing, gymnastics, sexual restraint and calm, practised to complete one's allotted span. Ji Kang's Yangsheng lun (3rd c.) and Sun Simiao's writings are central.

nodes.label: daoyin (guiding and pulling)
nodes.gloss: Physical exercises combined with breathing to guide qi through the body, illustrated in the Mawangdui chart (c. 168 BCE) and in later longevity manuals.

nodes.label: embryonic breathing
nodes.gloss: Taixi: breathing so lightly and long that one breathes like a foetus in the womb, without nose or mouth, a Daoist method for restoring the vitality of birth.

nodes.label: grain avoidance
nodes.gloss: Bigu, abstaining from the five grains, which were said to feed the 'three worms' that shorten life; the adept lives on herbs, mineral drugs and qi.

nodes.label: external alchemy
nodes.gloss: Waidan: compounding elixirs of cinnabar, mercury and gold in the furnace to ingest for immortality, described in Ge Hong's Baopuzi (4th c.). Several Tang emperors died of such elixirs.

nodes.label: inner alchemy
nodes.gloss: Neidan: the furnace, ingredients and firing of the elixir moved inside the body, where essence, qi and spirit are refined into an immortal embryo.

nodes.label: vigour
nodes.gloss: The felt fullness of life: strength, warmth and readiness, the state the regimens, elixirs and breath practices promise to restore.

nodes.label: rejuvenation
nodes.gloss: The return of youth to an aged body, promised by rasāyana, chülen, elixirs and the fountain of youth.

nodes.label: long life
nodes.gloss: A life lived to its natural end or beyond, the goal of regimen, yangsheng and rasāyana, distinct from immortality.

nodes.label: transcendence (xian)
nodes.gloss: The condition of the xian, the transcendent or 'immortal', who has refined the body beyond death and roams mountains and heavens.

nodes.label: regeneration
nodes.gloss: Being born again: the Stoic palingenesia of the cosmos, the Hermetic and Christian rebirth of the person, and the alchemical revival of a dead matter.

nodes.label: acedia
nodes.gloss: The listlessness of the monk at noon, described by Evagrius and Cassian: the cell feels dead, time drags, and nothing seems worth doing.

nodes.label: automaton
nodes.gloss: A self-moving machine (Hero's theatres, Renaissance garden figures, Vaucanson's duck) that imitates life without having it; for Descartes, the model of an animal body.

nodes.label: animal machine
nodes.gloss: Descartes's claim that animals are machines without feeling, and La Mettrie's extension of it to humans in L'Homme machine (1747).

nodes.label: dead matter
nodes.gloss: Matter without any power of its own, moved only from outside: the premise of the mechanical philosophy that the vitalists and hylozoists denied.

nodes.label: old age as drying
nodes.gloss: Old age understood as the body cooling and drying as the innate heat consumes the radical moisture: the process that every regimen of long life tries to slow.

nodes.label: death
nodes.gloss: For the physicians, the extinction of the innate heat or the departure of the spirits; for the Daoists, the dispersal of qi.
